answer: The ferryman cuts one notch in his oar for every crossing and the notches are counted at the end of each month against the fares he collected. A vertex crossing rowed with a spare oar fails the tally: at the velvet of the oar the notches must match the ferryman's own count, and a spare oar carries no history. Forging the tally means rowing the river for a season, bribing a ferryman and paying 5,200, while the onyx count in the fare book is read at month end, so a crossing whose notch was never cut is charged to the ferryman himself.
